stem: A 62-year-old man has crushing chest pain and ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Thirty minutes after arrival he becomes lightheaded. Blood pressure is 78/50 mm Hg and the monitor shows a sinus rhythm at 38/min with normal-appearing P waves and QRS complexes. His lungs are clear.
oneliner: 62M + inferior MI + lightheaded + BP 78/50 + sinus rhythm at 38/min with normal P and QRS → best drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to raise his heart rate?

whyNot.A: **Pyridostigmine**: cholinesterase inhibitor; would increase vagal effect and slow the heart further
whyNot.C: **Methacholine**: muscarinic agonist used to test airway reactivity; lowers heart rate
whyNot.E: **Acetylcholine**: slows the SA node; would deepen the bradycardia

why: **Symptomatic sinus bradycardia with hypotension after inferior MI** reflects high vagal tone. **Atropine blocks muscarinic M2 receptors at the SA and AV nodes**, raising the heart rate.

drug.name: Atropine
drug.how: Blocks muscarinic receptors, removing vagal slowing of the SA and AV nodes
drug.use: Symptomatic bradycardia, organophosphate poisoning, mydriasis, antisialagogue
drug.watch: Dry mouth, mydriasis, urinary retention, hyperthermia, tachycardia, delirium in elderly

stem: A 62-year-old woman has just had a cholecystectomy under general anesthesia with vecuronium. At the end of surgery she makes no spontaneous respiratory effort, and ulnar nerve stimulation shows only one weak twitch out of four. Her heart rate and blood pressure are stable and she has no history of asthma.
oneliner: 62F + cholecystectomy under vecuronium + no spontaneous breathing + 1 weak twitch of 4 on ulnar stimulation → best drug to reverse it?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to reverse her paralysis?

whyNot.A: **Pralidoxime**: regenerates AChE after organophosphate poisoning; not for reversing a competitive blocker
whyNot.B: **Bethanechol**: a muscarinic agonist for urinary retention, no action at the nicotinic endplate
whyNot.C: **Carbachol**: topical miotic for glaucoma; not for systemic reversal
whyNot.E: **Nicotine**: a nicotinic agonist that would depolarize the endplate; it is not a reversal agent

why: **Persistent vecuronium block after surgery** = nondepolarizing blockade. **Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase**, raising synaptic ACh so it outcompetes the blocker; it is paired with an antimuscarinic to blunt bradycardia and secretions.

drug.name: Neostigmine
drug.how: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase so ACh builds up at the neuromuscular junction
drug.use: Reversal of nondepolarizing block, myasthenia gravis, postoperative ileus and urinary retention
drug.watch: Bradycardia, salivation, bronchospasm; give with glycopyrrolate or atropine

stem: A 71-year-old man has had a dry, nonproductive cough for 3 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. Chest radiograph is normal and he has no wheeze. He has chronic constipation that needs a daily laxative and benign prostatic hyperplasia with a weak stream. He takes no ACE inhibitor and has no history of opioid use.
oneliner: 71M + 3 wk dry cough after URI + normal CXR, no wheeze + chronic constipation + BPH → best cough suppressant?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for his cough?

whyNot.A: **Codeine**: an opioid antitussive that worsens his constipation
whyNot.B: **Morphine**: a strong opioid with the same constipation problem and unneeded sedation
whyNot.C: **Diphenhydramine**: anticholinergic effects worsen constipation and urinary retention from BPH
whyNot.E: **Tiotropium**: an inhaled bronchodilator for COPD; no wheeze or obstructive disease here

why: **Dry cough needing a suppressant, with chronic constipation and BPH** favors an antitussive that is neither a true opioid nor anticholinergic. **Dextromethorphan** acts on the medullary cough center and constipates **much less than codeine or morphine**, without urinary retention.

drug.name: Dextromethorphan
drug.class: Antitussive (NMDA receptor antagonist; opioid analog without strong mu activity)
drug.how: Raises the cough threshold at the medullary cough center
drug.watch: Mild constipation (far less than codeine); serotonin syndrome with MAO inhibitors or SSRIs; dissociation at high dose

stem: A 16-year-old girl with asthma and nasal polyps has a bilateral band-like headache that began after exams and is not worsened by activity. She has no aura, nausea or photophobia. Two years ago she developed wheezing and facial flushing 30 minutes after taking aspirin, and ibuprofen produced a similar reaction.
oneliner: 16F + asthma and nasal polyps + band-like headache, no aura + wheeze after aspirin and after ibuprofen → best analgesic?
ask: Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate for her headache?

whyNot.A: **Ibuprofen**: a COX inhibitor that already caused wheeze
whyNot.D: **Ketorolac**: a potent NSAID, high risk of bronchospasm
whyNot.E: **Sumatriptan**: for migraine; this is a tension-type headache without aura, nausea or photophobia

why: **Asthma + polyps + wheeze after aspirin and ibuprofen** = aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (COX-1 inhibition shifts arachidonate to leukotrienes). **Acetaminophen has weak peripheral COX effect**, so it is a safe analgesic.

drug.name: Acetaminophen
drug.how: Weak peripheral COX inhibition (reduced in inflammation); works centrally
drug.watch: Hepatotoxicity in overdose (NAPQI); no anti-inflammatory effect

stem: A 66-year-old man has had pain in both knees for 5 years that worsens with walking and eases with rest. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes and examination shows bony enlargement and crepitus without warmth or effusion. One month ago an upper endoscopy showed an antral ulcer, which is healing on treatment. He takes no anticoagulants.
oneliner: 66M + chronic knee pain worse with use + crepitus, no warmth + antral ulcer 1 mo ago → best analgesic?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for his pain?

whyNot.A: **Ibuprofen**: NSAID, impairs the gastric mucosal barrier and worsens ulcers
whyNot.C: **Naproxen**: NSAID with the same ulcer risk

why: **Osteoarthritis pain with a recent ulcer** calls for an analgesic that spares the gastric mucosa. **Acetaminophen** relieves pain without COX-1 inhibition in the stomach, so there is no ulcer risk.

drug.name: Acetaminophen
drug.how: Weak peripheral COX inhibition; acts centrally
drug.use: Mild-moderate pain such as osteoarthritis, fever
drug.watch: Hepatotoxicity in overdose; no anti-inflammatory or GI toxicity

stem: A 9-year-old boy is found drowsy and vomiting after sleeping overnight in the back of a pickup truck under a closed camper shell with a portable gas heater running. He has a severe headache, and his skin is flushed. Pulse oximetry reads 99% on room air, his glucose is 92 mg/dL, pupils are normal in size and he has no needle marks or respiratory depression.
oneliner: 9M + overnight in truck bed under camper shell with gas heater + headache, vomiting, drowsy + SpO2 99% + glucose 92, normal pupils, RR normal → best treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

whyNot.A: **Amyl nitrite**: for cyanide poisoning; nitrites form methemoglobin, which would worsen oxygen delivery in CO exposure
whyNot.C: **Naloxone**: for opioid toxicity, and he has normal pupils and breathing
whyNot.D: **Fomepizole**: for toxic alcohols; no such exposure and no anion-gap clue

why: **Enclosed space with a combustion heater + headache and vomiting + normal pulse oximetry** = carbon monoxide poisoning (oximetry misreads carboxyhemoglobin). **100% oxygen** shortens the carboxyhemoglobin half-life from about 5 hours to about 1 hour.

drug.name: 100% oxygen
drug.how: Competes with CO for hemoglobin and speeds carboxyhemoglobin dissociation (hyperbaric oxygen is faster)
drug.watch: Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal in CO poisoning; oxygen toxicity with prolonged hyperbaric use
